item.title: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: China
item.description: Part 4 of the Web Accessibility Deep Dive post series - this time taking look at China.
item.content:encoded:
Intro

Hi all! This post continues the series Web Accessibility Deep Dive and follows my post on India in Web Accessibility Deep Dive: India.

I chose China as a wild card for this series because it’s insulated enough from my corner of the world that I would assume that it might be the least affected by the decisions made by governments I must regularly interact with. My guess is that if I’m looking for a state to take a distinct approach, China would be most at liberty to do so.

Outside of one time that I was trying to understand the documentation for a laser etching machine’s proprietary software, this might be the first time I’ve properly ventured into territory where I can’t read much of the relevant documentation. In this case, I’ve had to take a more circuitous route when I can’t find what I’m looking for. Thankfully, university research papers (one) exist!

Development

To start, two organizations come up regularly concerning China’s efforts towards accessibility: the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the China Disabled Persons’ Federation (CDPF).

The legal foundation starts with the Law on the Protection of Persons with Disabilities 1990, as amended in 2008, which has two notable articles that have implications on web accessibility as well as enforcement guidelines:

  • Article 44 discusses the state’s intentions to encourage and assist disabled people’s participation in creative pursuits.
  • Article 54 discusses the state’s intentions to remove barriers to communication and public information, and to develop technology and products suitable for those with disabilities. It specifically mentions assistance for the visually impaired regarding entrance examinations.
  • Section VIII describes the rights of disabled persons to seek assistance in investigation, filing lawsuits, and applying for arbitration in the case that their rights are infringed. It also outlines consequences for those that delay those actions or otherwise violate the dignity of disabled people.

This essentially provides a framework for people to start making their needs known and getting assistance to have them met, creating a grounds for more specific recommendations to grow in the following years.

The Technical Requirements for Web Accessibility (YD/T 1761-2008) was approved in 2008 and to my best understanding was updated in 2012 to pull in some elements of WCAG 2.0. To be clear, the text “WCAG” does not appear in the standard - it instead elects to write each item out, for example explicitly including the “perceivable” principle added in WCAG 2.0. More recently China approved the Information Technology requirements and Testing Methods for Accessibility of Web Content (GB/T 37668-2019) standard which references WCAG 2.0 and 2.1. As with other standards, enforcement comes later.

The Guiding Opinions of the China Disabled Persons’ Federation on Promoting Information Accessibility MIIT GXBLXG [2020] No. 146 and the Implementation Plan to Help the Elderly Use Digital Technologies (State Council No.45) resulted in the Special Action Plan on Transforming Internet Apps For Better Access by Senior and People with Disabilities MIIT GXBLXG [2020] No. 200, which specifies a list of websites which must be made accessible by 2021 ranging from government sites to shopping and entertainment. The approach is fairly focused as far as disability legislation goes, pledging increased development and implementation of standards for disabled people as well as going into detail about targeting the needs of older users. It rewards successes with displayable badges and assigns penalties to organizations’ Enterprise Credit Evaluation for failing to meet requirements on time.

In 2023 China implemented the Barrier-Free Environment Construction Law (no alias) which outlines accessibility requirements for new construction, enhancements, and how information is distributed. As of 2025, a State Council Information Office press conference claimed, in addition to other barrier removals, that over 3000 websites and mobile apps had undergone accessibility modifications.

We’ll now look at the paper I found. Typically I’d do a few things to vet a research paper, but in this case I cannot do anything but gesture at Tsinghua University and the word “published”, so on we go! Enqiao Gu’s research article, Before and After the Barrier-Free Law: Legal Implementation of Accessibility in China, discusses the environment preceding the law as well as its reception. They cite criticisms of prior legislation, including that it was often softly worded and featured disconnects between who was granted the power to enforce legislation and what offices actually existed to do so. Given my prior post on India, it may be stating the obvious to suggest that this is a common issue with developing legislation that I’ll see continue the more I pry.

Prior legislation had issued from different administrative bodies and by merit of being issued by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress the Barrier-Free Law has a lot more legislative power behind it and has predictably resulted in more action, especially in regard to the creation of supplementary material and discussion. The Barrier-Free Law particularly cares about the adherence of organizations providing public information and transportation, telecommunications providers, and anything regarding emergency services, and takes steps to reduce and remove a previously perpetuated disparity between urban and rural accessibility requirements.

Enforcement includes fines for specific types of failures but power to take action largely falls on the government; individuals are limited in options to self-advocate via the court system. It’s also not complete from my perspective - there are a lot of entities that are in the grey area for required compliance depending on how public spaces are defined, and a lot of private sector entities that are out of scope. Enqiao Gu speculates that this gap could be filled with social law - law of incentives and cooperation, rather than a more administrative or punitive one.

Since this is fairly recent, I imagine that follow-up is to come.

Returning to my initial assumption that China might be a good wild card - was it warranted? Did I get some neat alternative approach to WCAG to read through? Aside from earlier documents - no. China is throwing their support towards development of the same global standard (WCAG). However, the state does put an emphasis on accessibility as it pertains to the needs of the elderly. Given that we all live longer and longer, assuming seniors will be occupying the same space and environments and granting them the tools and independence to do so as much as possible can only help in the long run. Peeking ahead to the scaffolding of following posts I actually don’t see this approach frequently, so yes, it was definitely worthwhile.

As a final side note, I found this handbook on media reporting while I was trying to find relevant documents pertaining to China and I think it’s a great read. It discusses the framing of disability in news reporting and I think it has pretty widespread tie-ins about how how our modes of thinking and speaking impact communities at scale.

Next

My plan is for this series to continue with the EU and UK!

Links

  • Law on the Protection of Persons with Disabilities via CDPF: http://english.cdpf.org.cn/2017-07/30/c_914832.htm
  • Law on the Protection of Disabled Persons via UNESCO: https://media.unesco.org/sites/default/files/webform/r2e002/c8c673b9a684f2a77cdca091a95100259ccf26dd.pdf
  • Ruoxi Ran’s W3 Blog on GB/T 37668-2019: https://www.w3.org/blog/2020/updated-chinese-accessibility-standard/
  • YD/T 1761-2012: https://www.chinesestandard.net/PDF.aspx/YDT1761-2012
  • Baidu’s Review of Chinese accessibility advances: https://baike.baidu.com/item/%E7%BD%91%E9%A1%B5%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E6%97%A0%E9%9A%9C%E7%A2%8D/8126897
  • CDPF: http://english.cdpf.org.cn/2023-08/29/c_914622.htm
  • UNESCO on Disability in Media Reporting: https://articles.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2024/04/Handbook%20on%20Media%20Reporting%20for%20Promoting%20Disability%20Equality%20in%20China%20%281%29.pdf
  • State Council No. 45: https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/wpro---documents/countries/china/policy-docs/implementation-plan-to-help-the-elderly-use-digital-technologies.pdf?sfvrsn=f77270c5_3
  • MIIT GXBLXG [2020] No. 146: https://www.miit.gov.cn/jgsj/xgj/scgl/art/2020/art_eca74f5b0c4a493e9e466195bd71ec74.html
  • MIIT GXBLXG [2020] No. 200: https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/wpro---documents/countries/china/policy-docs/special-action-plan-on-transforming-internet-apps.pdf?sfvrsn=8eb37ac5_3
  • Barrier-Free Environment Construction Law: https://www.gov.cn/yaowen/liebiao/202306/content_6888910.htm
  • 2025 SCIO Press Conference: http://english.scio.gov.cn/m/pressroom/2025-07/23/content_117991950.html
  • Enqiao Gu’s Research on the Barrier-Free Law: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/383343052_Before_and_After_the_Barrier-Free_Law_Legal_Implementation_of_Accessibility_in_China

item.title: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: India
item.description: Part 3 of my series on Web Accessibility, taking a look at developments in India.
item.content:encoded:
Intro

Hi all! Continuing the post series Web Accessibility Deep Dive and following up on the introduction to this segment on the legal landscape of web accessibility in Web Accessibility Deep Dive: Legislation Lifecycles & The UN, we’re going to take a look at India.

I think it would be an understatement to say that there is anything less than a highway of technical expertise and practices between India, Canada, and the USA. Ideas in one will osmose to the others, and India is very much carving out more and more real estate in software and the decisions impacting those that use it. I will begin here.

Development

To start, in the 90’s India joined what we’ll later see is a massive wave of disability rights legislation by passing The Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995 (PWD 1995). This act outlines the rights of disabled people, including the rights to non-discrimination, employment, education, and transportation, as well as declaring its intent to support research and affirmative action initiatives. It also requires that institutions for disabled people are registered according to the act.

In 2009 India began publishing guidelines for the quality and accessibility of government websites with the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps (GIGW). These guidelines are broad in scope, and successive iterations include a focus on web accessibility and cybersecurity.

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD) provided necessary follow-up to the prior works as well as the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Chapter VIII Section 40 requires accessible information and communication, facilities, and services regardless of location and Section 42 specifically mentions the right to accessible media and every day electronic devices. This law is notable among others because it is legally enforceable across the public and private sector and in Section 90 it allows leadership to be held accountable if the case of violations if they are found to be knowingly neglectful. It is administered by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities.

GIGW was iterated on in 2019 with GIGW 2.0 adding support for WCAG 2.0 and then again in 2023 with GIGW 3.0 updating to reference WCAG 2.1 as well as adding a plethora of other guidelines in addition to accessibility regarding application quality, cybersecurity, and lifecycle management. GIGW 3.0 is a product of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).

Also hitting the books in 2021 and 2022, the Indian standard Accessibility for the ICT Products and Services (IS 17802 Part 1 & Part 2) provided specifics for accessibility compliance as well as how those would be evaluated. Since this is described as a living document it is likely to be updated over time, but at time of writing it cites WCAG 2.1. Because this standard is backed by the RPwD, it is applicable across many sectors.

The question is, are these laws actually enforced? The answer is that they are being enforced very inconsistently depending on where you are but the wheels are currently turning to change this. A key part of enforcing the RPwD is the appointment of a State Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, whose role it is to essentially ensure follow up on compliance with the act. Without one of these, there isn’t really an easy way for a person with disabilities to pursue recourse if they are discriminated against. So, while it was the law for resources on the web to be accessible and that law was enforceable on paper, in some cases there wasn’t anyone around to do so. Also absent was a good way to collect penalties if they were deemed appropriate under Section 89 of RPwD, making enforcement doubly difficult.

In July of this year, India’s Supreme Court made a move to correct this and ordered that ten states and union territories (there are 28 states and 8 union territories total) that had not yet done so appoint State Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities, including Delhi and Karnataka. This article on HalfAccessible goes into great detail and provides necessary context, including how developments in the court case Rajive Raturi v Union of India (Diary Number 9321/2005) have played into this additional ruling (and disability legislation in general). Essentially, at the end of 2024 the Supreme Court found that the standards referenced in Rule 15 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules (RPwDR) were phrased too flexibly as guidelines, resulting in inconsistent enforcement and subverting the intent of the RPwD, which was to provide a baseline of accessibility that could be developed over time.

They threw Rule 15 out and then in July of this year provided a 4 week deadline to get enforcers ready to go and a 6 month deadline to re-evaluate accessibility standards. It wouldn’t be a bad idea to monitor the news in India around the turn of the year as this is ongoing.

Next

The series will continue with a post on web accessibility in China, which is now up: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: China

Links

  • PWD Act: https://media.unesco.org/sites/default/files/webform/r2e002/42fc9808f00926c6b43390588c83ba0e8d7addfc.pdf
  • DEPWD & RPwD Content: https://depwd.gov.in/en/acts/
  • GIGW 3.0: https://guidelines.india.gov.in/introduction/
  • IS 17802 Part 1 Requirements: https://archive.org/details/gov.in.is.17802.1.2021/mode/1up
  • IS 17802 Part 2 Determination of Conformance: https://archive.org/details/gov.in.is.17802.2.2022/mode/1up
  • July 29 2026 Supreme Court Order: https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2005/9321/9321_2005_6_301_72783_Order_29-Jul-2026.pdf
  • HalfAccessible on RPwD Developments: https://halfaccessible.com/rpwd-act-disability-rights-india-supreme-court/
  • Rajive Raturi v Union of India: https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2005/9321/9321_2005_1_1503_56986_Judgement_08-Nov-2024.pdf
  • RPwDR: https://thc.nic.in/Central%20Governmental%20Rules/Rights%20of%20Persons%20with%20Disabilities%20Rules,%202017.pdf

item.title: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: Legislation Lifecycles & The UN
item.description: Part 2 of my series on Web Accessibility, starting with what we're looking for in legislation as well as developments in the UN.
item.content:encoded:
Intro

Hi all! This is a follow up from my first post in this series: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: Intro. In this segment of the series I’ll go over the history of legislation concerning web accessibility, including some general disability and human rights developments. It ended up being fairly long so I’ll be breaking it into multiple posts for readability. Details on standards, compliance, and tools (the HOW to do accessibility) will follow later.

Oftentimes people go into specific fields because of their background - they think XYZ field can help them contribute in some way. Early on in my software career I came to the conclusion that the tools I build should make other people’s work and lives better, easier, or more enjoyable, so - full disclosure - this post is from the perspective of someone that wants laws and practices that serve those ends. Since I’ve lived in Canada and the USA my focus will be there, but for perspective I’ll be casting a wide net both geographically and topically. As I write my post there are a few different potentially relevant political upheavals occurring and the potential for a Canadian “Associate” status within the EU, so this approach feels more and more appropriate as I go.

My Process

The blog series as a whole is exploratory for me but since this specific topic deals in more concrete, fact-heavy information as opposed to personal experimentation and experience I’m taking a different approach than I’ve done elsewhere.

This is the first time I’ve tried to write anything approaching an academic level of rigor since college a little over a decade ago and I find the environment has changed quite a lot since then. As I watch news, read discourse on social media, and read articles written in an authoritative tone on this and tangentially related topics, I find I’ve made some assumptions about what’s expected. Instead of documented, verifiable paper trails, I see researchers arguing about whether or not they can write with AI. I see people positioning themselves as authorities saying that you can just tell the AI not to hallucinate, silly. I see articles discussing the implications of law that don’t cite or so much as link back to copies of the documents they discuss. Not to be “back in my day…” and all but the bar appears to be being jerked around a bit.

This post takes a bit of a relative middle ground. I’m gathering as many quality resources as I can, especially the legislation in question, but I often haven’t noted the lines in documents that I’m basing my statements on as I’m aggregating and writing. This isn’t academic, but it’s not unaccountable either. I’m avoiding sources that I feel are untrustworthy, which includes:

  • Sources that don’t help me find copies of documents they discuss
  • Sources that aren’t affiliated with authorities in the space or news
  • Anything that looks to be based in AI

I’ve got an Obligatory AI Post on the books for later, but as of right now, suffice it to know that I don’t think AI sources constitute citation material outside of the self-referential. However, I can’t say I’ve successfully avoided unreliable information. If I can’t read a document, who is to say the articles and translations I’ve deferred to are based in legitimate interpretations? raggle fraggle We learn, I guess.

The Recipe for Success

Before I start, please note that several types of documents will be discussed. Each state will handle their legal approach slightly differently, but from my recent reading this is how these documents tend to be defined:

  • Policies generally regard a state’s intentions but do not provide concrete practices to be followed and are not enforceable. For example, a party can have policy before their candidates are even elected.
  • Laws and Acts go further than policy - they say that the state will enforce certain behaviors, but they do not necessarily have to describe how to do this. Laws that are too vague are difficult to enforce and may result in confusion in court systems or whatever bodies are charged with interpreting them. This is why regulations often come later.
  • Standards outline specific practices that can be followed and are often developed by independent organizations.
  • Regulations outline the enforcement of laws, and in our case will likely cite a given standard to adhere to.

In my experience terms like “law” and “policy” seem to be used to refer to miscellaneous legislation regardless of enforceability in less formal settings but “regulation” doesn’t appear to be thrown around as carelessly.

As I understand it policy is a gesture and laws and standards get the ball rolling, but applicable regulations are what are needed to enforce accessibility in a given jurisdiction. You also need data and the funding to collect it - you can’t tell if your regulations are doing anything without data. Essentially, you get a pattern that looks like this:

Sentiment –> Policy –> Laws –> Research, Standards, Lawsuits –> Regulations

Additionally, we care about who these documents apply to - sometimes they only apply to government affiliated organizations or contractors. However, in order to have a properly accessible society enough employers and businesses must adhere to these standards that those needing services within the accessibility ecosystem have real choices outside of “which one can I even use?” Accessibility endgame isn’t about offering a product or public service that can be used correctly one way and then a premium alternative to those people with disabilities that need it, it’s about making the assumption that humans will need to interact with their environments in a variety of ways and building that way first, across the board. This is called Universal Design.

Development by Jurisdiction

In the following sections I’ll go a bit more into detail on the actions of specific bodies. I’ll start with the United Nations and then in following posts take a look at the European Union and a selection of countries which I picked based on their relevance to me and those entities I am most likely to interact with.

The United Nations Directives and The CRPD

The United Nations is a body that facilitates diplomacy. Its output is declarations and treaties, and it functions because sometimes states do what they say they will. The declarations that are made aren’t binding - they are more in line with what I understand policy to be - but the treaties that follow are binding in the sense that they are promises that states make to one another that can then be pointed to later as evidence of good or bad faith.

Disability legislation is one such case where there was follow-through; declarations led to a treaty that was signed and in turn led to real legislation.

The United Nations work concerning disability goes all the way back to The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR or General Assembly Resolution 217 A) of 1948. In this declaration, Article 2 specifies that everyone, without distinction of any kind, is entitled to the rights outlined in the document. Article 25 specifies a right to an adequate standard of living and security in times of need, including disability. Article 27 specifies a right to participate in culture, art, and benefit from scientific advancements. Reading through this document almost 80 years after its release, it’s more than a little sad that we still haven’t achieved much of what this document aspired to. Opposition and slow adoption of human rights stances advanced by a new and not-entirely-accepted body such as the UN could be taken into context and understood or we could say “this is human rights, they should have been here yesterday, why on Earth are we prioritizing things other than having human rights yesterday?” We need both attitudes in order to make progress. It’ll just have to be the work of more than one lifetime.

In 1975, the UN got a bit more specific, issuing the Declaration on the Rights of Disabled Persons (A/RES/3447(XXX)) which declares that people with disabilities have the same fundamental rights as “fellow-citizens of the same age… to enjoy a decent life, as normal and full as possible” and that therefore their needs should be taken account in economic and social planning, they should be protected from discrimination and exploitation, and that they should be able to take legal action in their defense. As we will see, legislation does follow! During this time we get early disability rights protections and the first standards.

However, this wasn’t enough.

Three decades later, in 2006 the UN held the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD or A/RES/61/106). During this convention, member states agreed that people with disabilities were being denied basic rights and that legislation was required to enshrine said rights. In our case the most relevant right is the right to access information. In Chapter 5 it is made clear that said legislation should grant disabled people the right to seek legal recourse for infringements and for appropriate resources to be available to support that endeavor. Finally, it establishes a multi-national committee to follow up - the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

This convention was key because member states that ratified it were obliged to implement (or otherwise directly adhere to, if their legal system permits) the above legislation and several states that follow here have cited it as a direct reason for doing so. As we will see, its expectations are in fact viewed as obligatory.

At time of writing,164 out of 194 member states have signed the CRPD. Record is kept of signing date and any statements on the UN treaty depositary.

Next

The series continues with a look at India in Web Accessibility Deep Dive: India.

Links

  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights
  • UN Early Disability History: https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/history-of-united-nations-and-persons-with-disabilities-the-decade-of-the-nineties.html
  • 1993 SREOPD: https://www.un.org/esa/socdev/enable/dissre00.htm
  • CRPD Convention Overview: https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/resources/handbook-for-parliamentarians/handbook-for-parliamentarians-on-the
  • CRPD Committee: https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/crpd
  • CRPD Overview (Canadian Source): https://lop.parl.ca/sites/PublicWebsite/default/en_CA/ResearchPublications/201309E
  • UNDIS 1.0 Summary: https://unsdg.un.org/resources/system-wide-evaluation-un-disability-inclusion-strategy-terms-reference
  • UNDIS 2.0 Summary: https://www.un.org/en/disabilitystrategy
  • UN CRPD Ratification Record: https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=IV-15&chapter=4&clang=_en

item.title: IBM DevOps Training - Early Thoughts
item.description: In the summer of 2026, I decided to set up my good friends Development and Operations on a blind date.
item.content:encoded:
Intro

A short while ago I decided to pursue the IBM DevOps and Software Engineering Certificate. I did this for a few very predictable reasons:

  • Technology is always changing, and practitioners must follow suit.
  • DevOps methodologies in particular are relevant to me as they are an iteration on practices I utilized in a previous role.
  • In addition to methods, this training makes use of tools spanning the full range of development - some of which I haven’t used before.

This training is estimated to take around 6 months if the trainee puts in around 10 hours a week. As I go, I’m going to document my thoughts here and in follow-up posts.

My Context Going Into This

While the technology stacks that various organizations use to approach their design challenges are heterogeneous, the strategies they throw at their respective software development lifecycles seem to chase homogeneity. Of the roles I’ve recently applied for, around a third mention Agile. Around a tenth mention the SDLC and/or DevOps. None mention Waterfall (I’d be surprised). Last week one mentioned GitOps! In some ways, these work like fads - a new technique for organizing work will come out and a lead or manager will shave off weeks or years of development time and then every organization has to restructure. Will the trend-setters slow down as methods are perfected? Could there be some foundational misunderstanding about work that causes us to throw all of these methods out one day in favor of something else? Who knows! In the scheme of things, the Industrial Revolution and the following events that kicked a lot of this into motion happened basically yesterday.

Since my longest role was with a Very Large Company™ with complex team structures and interconnected applications that must work in conjunction with one another, I think it comes as no surprise to the reader that I’m familiar with Agile. I was formally trained in Agile Scrum, but on later discussions with my team’s scrum master about how our actual process deviated from the standard (the self-organizing aspects were a bit more top down, and we had this thing called a release train) he agreed that our process wasn’t standard Scrum and looked a little more like the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe).

To go back further, my first encounter with Agile was seeing the manifesto open on a coworker’s workstation. I can’t recall if he was considering pitching it to the rest of the team or satiating personal curiosity. I have fond memories from that role, but I can’t say I learned a “development process”. I can’t say the team even used Waterfall because the sites we were working with were at least a decade into maintenance. Looking back, my two cents is that the team was small and Kanban would have sufficed for keeping tasks moving in maintenance. Also, I hope they use version control now. Oh-ho-ho yes, there was no version control! We had the power of prayer in that shop.

Early on, the reception I recall was that developers hated the amount of meetings it added to their day. I also dislike meetings… if they are inefficient. Agile caught on regardless of this because when applied to the scenarios it was designed for, it works.

Initial Comments on the Training

To get started, I need to answer what kind of problem DevOps is meant to solve, and in what way that deviates from what I’m used to.

Agile is all about getting a demoable project in front of stakeholders as early on in the development process as possible so that feedback can be gained and direction can be changed in order to minimize time and resource wastage and then iterating on that.

Once that code is written, it’s not done - the code has got to go somewhere, be built, tested, revised, rebuilt, retested, accepted, deployed, and maintained. This is the part that isn’t always correctly addressed with Agile alone. This occurs because often, development is one person or team’s responsibility, and the responsibility of all-that-other-stuff goes to other people or teams. The problem is silos.

DevOps aims to integrate these silos, including the ALL of the specialties that go into a given project are co-located on a more expanded idea of a fully cross-functional team. This includes developers, QA, operations, everyone relevant, and extends throughout the project’s life. The people developing it need to be the people operating and maintaining it. The remainder is process optimization - if development is meant to go fast, how do we make that happen, and how do we keep fast from equaling sloppy? DevOps says the answer to this is automation - for its speed, for its consistency - applied to building, testing, deploy, and monitoring of the entire architecture.

The training itself covers the theory and methods as well as the various tools that support this. For me, this means a review of Agile and cloud from IBM’s perspective (my introduction was with AWS). It also includes an abundance of other tools and methods spanning CI/CD. Some of which I’m very familiar with, some parts I’ve only had indirect involvement with professionally, and some that I haven’t touched entirely.

The Topic

The training opens with an overview of what DevOps is. My gut response is that it feels exactly like the Agile training I had a few years ago - I’m being sold a product. The tools are products,. The culture is a product which reinforces itself and requires training, which is also a product.

Products have applications, markets, etc. so the key to buying correctly is understanding the market it’s for, what correct application looks like and when it’s appropriate, as well as if there are competitors and when, if ever, they are better.

The Delivery

The training starts with the conditions surrounding the birth of DevOps. Particularly the who, the when, and the why. For me, usually details like “proper noun was done/said/written by this person on this date” aren’t easily retained. Repetition doesn’t really help unless it is spaced out over a period of time, usually longer than standardized testing can account for. Let’s consider that I’m good at learning a few things:

  • Fine motor skills, particularly regarding crafts
  • Understanding a technique, especially how something is constructed, painted, or otherwise comes together
  • Understanding narratives and motivations, parsing possible dynamics between people and things, walking through cause and effect, and making predictions based on examples I’ve seen If we make the thing I’m bad at more like the thing I’m good at, we can succeed at retaining random facts! In this case, I have to have a narrative. To the instructor’s credit he did frame the early evolution of DevOps as a narrative, but it was a very Cliffnotes-ed version and with too many proper nouns in quick succession and not as much plot. The result was that I ended up doing far more reading on each individual bullet point thrown in front of me than I imagine the training includes in its time estimate in order to retain the contents of those bullet points and place them in their context.

That first topic is fortunately brief, the training basically states that the founders and their actions and materials are primarily discussed in order to emphasize that the methodology comes from workers and practitioners and not random spitballing administrators. Understood. I drilled it enough to pass the quizzes and moved on. Later content has had similar issues when it comes to engaging my insatiable rock-flipping, but fortunately is more about processes and techniques and hasn’t featured as many names or dates.

💡 Since I'm doing a lot of side reading I think the training will be more of a time investment than it estimates. In this case, this isn't a bad thing. Each of these topics are valuable, and it means that I'm interested in what I'm learning.

The training makes frequent use of quizzes with multiple choice questions - *Gasp*. The questions are often worded weirdly, which comes with the territory. Multiple choice is popular because it is easy to configure and easy to score, so I’ll leave that as it is. Aside from that, there’s been one instance so far where the content review for a section involved having a discussion with an LLM. It’s 2026 - I’ve read plenty about LLMs, interacted with them briefly in a few contexts, and discussed them with those that build and train them, but it was fascinating and eerie to experience the sycophancy in a longer duration conversation firsthand. I expect that I’ll encounter this evaluation method again.

It looks like later material will be more hands-on. This is why I picked Coursera - you really can’t replace hands-on experience. Early on in the training, an account feature code is generated for accessing student cloud resources, but my code is invalid and customer support hasn’t addressed my issue yet. I’m 2 tickets in, yay! We’ll see how that goes, but I’ll look into alternative means to access the resources if necessary because the practical experience is valuable to me.

Final Thoughts (For Now)

So far I’ve completed the Introduction to DevOps course, and am most of the way through Introduction to Cloud Computing. Has anything changed? A little. Going into this I was under the impression DevOps was about automation and doing CI/CD. I’ve had conversations with friends in tech that discuss DevOps as if it is a role someone can have or a team. Now, I understand the first impression is sort of accurate, but doesn’t really capture the picture of why it’s used and the problem it’s trying to solve. I was lacking in context. The second impression now feels like it could be counterproductive outright if it creates the silos that DevOps practices are supposed to remove. The cloud section has been almost entirely review - there’s been some “ah did I understand that the same way the first time through” or “wait, AWS and IBM must do XYZ differently…” moments, but they’ve been rare.

Since I’m still early on in this training, my opinions are still developing. Updates to follow.

Links

  • Agile Manifesto - https://agilemanifesto.org/
  • Scrum.org (the formal training I did at my last role) - https://www.scrum.org/
  • SAFe - https://framework.scaledagile.com/
  • GitOps - https://www.gitops.tech/
  • Amazon on the SDLC - https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/sdlc/
  • IBM on DevOps - https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/devops
  • GitHub on CI/CD - https://github.com/resources/articles/ci-cd

item.title: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: Intro
item.description: Part 1 of my series on Web Accessibility. Let's outline our starting point for this series on accessibility.
item.content:encoded:
Intro

Accessibility is one of those topics that is often looked at in a very narrow sense, and only after a concern is raised, a complaint has been lodged, or money has been lost. I think that there is a critical reason behind this:

Organizations aren’t framing what accessibility is correctly, and therefore don’t understand its value.

Accessibility is the degree of usability for all users, especially taking into account those with differing needs. At scale this applies to the spaces, services, devices, and technology that we interact with. All of it. The practice of making a given thing (in my case, software) accessible starts with considering how it will be practically used, and how different users will either need or want to approach its use.

For example, users may have:

  • Limited mobility
  • Limited use of their hands
  • Slow reaction time
  • Limited senses like sight, hearing, or smell
  • A tendency for motion sickness
  • Discomfort at extreme or uncontrollable sensory input
  • Language barriers, including dialect, slang, or jargon
  • Cognitive impairment

Consider that accessibility can vary by the device being used. A site that is accessible on desktop may not be on Android or iOS.

Lastly, even if it isn’t the primary target, it can be useful to consider that even if a user doesn’t have a disability, they may need or prefer to use your invention in unconventional ways. For example, if a user has disruptive responsibilities - think children - they may have difficulty completing tasks in one sitting. In that case, allowing users to save form data or pause an activity could go a long way. I don’t have kids but I could imagine how such a thing could assist me - think of how many times you may have accidentally refreshed an involved form and then had to refill it, or clicked a supplementary document on a page only to find out you clicked away from the page and lost all your progress. Improving accessibility raises the standard for everyone, not just the targeted communities.

I’ll say this because you likely do not know me - I think that we should seek to ensure that the things we make are widely accessible even if the money incentive isn’t there, but I’m going to stand on the hill that I believe an incentive IS there. If you make a product or provide a service that is better for some, nine times out of ten it’ll make a product or service that is better for all.

I don’t like flashing lights, movement, noise, or often even bright colors. If I’m surprised by these things, I may struggle to process how to remove them quickly, and I’ll run from your site rather than try to figure out how. This is an entirely reasonable response!

Standards and Enforcers

Accessibility is enforced by community guidelines as well as legal standards. Community organizations like the A11y Project, IAAP, and W3C gather and share information to determine the best methods to advance accessibility initiatives, outlined in documents like WCAG.

Governments outline laws to define how their internal organizations must operate, according to government disability and accessibility initiatives at the time. For example:

  • The European Accessibility Act - a 2019 directive consolidating accessibility laws across the European Union
  • The Accessible Canada Act (ACA) and various province-level acts, in my case AODA
  • The Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 508

There are often exceptions to these legal requirements, but it is important to keep in mind that even if legal consequences are not applicable, a bad user experience due to accessibility failures will drive at least some users away.

Resources & Auditing Tools

There are organizations that provide guidance and resources in addition to the organizations listed above which contributed to WCAG:

  • WebAIM - Utah State University’s Institute for Disability Research
  • Microsoft Learn - probably all of the big CSPs will have relevant courses
  • Accessibility Services Canada - funded by Ontario govt, provides paid courses and a nice list of resources

Paid courses are offered by many colleges and organizations selling compliance training, but since I am currently paying for Coursera that’s where I’m most likely to spend time first.

Many site builders are beginning to include accessibility checks in their toolkits, but dedicated tools are also available to perform accessibility audits on other sites:

  • Accessibilitychecker.org - reviews your website’s source code against guidelines
  • Chrome Lighthouse - Google’s auditing tool, provides performance and accessibility reviews
  • WAVE - WebAIM’s auditing tool
  • Silktide - full UX auditing tool with paid and free options

What is to Follow

This, more or less, was the state of my notes after I spent a day or so looking into accessibility in 2025. That wasn’t my first encounter - I’ve familiarized myself with web accessibility concepts as they pertain to my work in the past but this foray made it clear that said concepts aren’t the full picture. This isn’t the whole ball game; it’s the first throw, and it can be taken in a few different directions in the posts to follow:

  • What are the specific requirements of the laws and guidelines listed above and how would I go about meeting them?
  • How does the legal landscape differ, both between the US, CA, and the EU as well as at the province level?
  • For that matter, what about other countries? Businesses are global, the things I will work with may need to be utilized elsewhere. Accessibility applies to location as well.
  • In what way are the laws potentially deficient? Should I build things that exceed them?
  • Explore auditing: how do each of the auditing tools above work, and when should I use them? Are there other tools? Are there ways in which the tools fail to assess accessibility?

Continue reading here with my introduction to the web accessibility legal landscape and developments in the United Nations: Web Accessibility Deep Dive: Legislation Lifecycles & The UN.

Links

  • A11y Project: https://www.a11yproject.com/
  • IAAP: https://www.accessibilityassociation.org/
  • WCAG: https://www.wcag.com/resource/what-is-wcag/
  • WCAG W3: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/
  • Mozilla’s Guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/Accessibility
  • WebAim: https://webaim.org/

Laws

  • European Accessibility Act: https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/european-accessibility-act-eaa_en
  • Accessible Canada Act: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/a-0.6/
  • Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities: https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/05a11)
  • Americans with Disabilities Act: https://www.ada.gov/topics/intro-to-ada/
  • Section 508: (https://www.section508.gov/)
  • ADA Design Standards: https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/design-standards/

Video

  • Imran Siddiq’s 2025 overview of the legal landscape surrounding accessibility and some of what will be required: The deadline is running out for Web Accessibility

item.title: A Linux Migration
item.description: Recently I've been wondering if I should continue using Windows for my personal projects or try something else.
item.content:encoded:
Priorities

For quite a long time, I’ve been a Windows user. I paint, I game, I use Microsoft staples like Visual Studio and Office. At work my story is more of the same, with the addition of Microsoft 365 and Teams. I’d say I’ve gotten pretty complacent with my apps just working and Windows Defender taking care of preventing potential nasties from running loose on my machine.

Lately, I’ve been a bit less content with that arrangement. Like media, tools have audiences or intended user bases. Tools as they are designed make assumptions about their users and cater to those assumptions. Windows assumes that its users prioritize convenience and are willing to exchange increasing degrees of autonomy and data for it. You can tinker with how Windows operates, but tinker-ability isn’t its priority. If you are living in the Windows ecosystem you likely aren’t really thinking about alternative desktops or audio or video drivers. Over the last few years I’ve come to value these things which are less prioritized more and more.

Alternatives

This brings me to alternatives. I’ve used macOS on a few occasions for media and app development, and while it is nice for both I wouldn’t say it satisfies my desire for tinkering. This leaves Linux-based operating systems, which have apparently changed dramatically since my college Unix and Ubuntu course in 2012 or 2013. From my position on the periphery, it seemed to have the reputation of being for specific development or infrastructure uses only. Scary! Not for beginners!

A decade later I am both not a beginner and the Linux space has become a lot more varied in what it offers, how it markets itself, and who it is for. Top 10 lists of distributions include suggestions for users coming from Windows or macOS, users that want to game, and those pursuing creative projects. If anything is discouraging, it is the overabundance of choice. Casually wiki-diving for the distributions and tech available, you can quickly end up with a map that looks like this:

I built this map slowly over the course of months, and I can see how to someone else looking to get started with a migration it might look like a massive learning curve. I’ll boil down what I’ve learned to a couple statements that are both more representative and more optimistic:

  1. Learning as you go is perfectly fine
  2. You should play with your tech, your PC is probably not going to explode
  3. If you install something and don’t like it, try something else

Scooting on Over

Once I’d filled in my charts and become a SME Once I’d decided I should just get on with it, I needed to tinker, specifically to install and run one of these distributions. The first step was identifying which apps I could bring with me and which ones you I couldn’t. In my case, the only real casualty was Corel Painter, which used .riff files which I had to convert to something I could open with another app. I also used Scrivener, but Wine translation was available for it so in theory I’d be safe to leave those files be. I backed everything I cared about up.

I decided on a few options based on the following priorities:

  • Versatility, it should be good for entertainment AND work
  • Favor popular and supported distros to build confidence
  • Customization should be encouraged

For me that resulted in 3 options:

  1. Linux Mint for its friendliness to Windows users
  2. Pop!_OS for its friendliness to games and my NVIDIA GPU
  3. Fedora on recommendation from a developer friend

There are 3 ways to run a secondary operating system: live boot from a USB, dual booting, and running in a VM, each with their own limitations. Briefly:

  1. Local VMs are low commitment and good for quickly trying out many options but tend to be slow and limited in what hardware they can access
  2. Live USBs are portable and can fully utilize hardware but require lightweight operating systems or else they will be slow
  3. Dual booted OSs have full access to resources and will be the best performing but require a committed installation

My first experiment was with Mint: I ran it from a flash drive and surprise, surprise - Mint was slow. Not because Mint is slow, but because it was an inappropriate choice for a live USB. It was also familiar. I spent enough time poking around the desktop and menus to realize that maybe, with this change, I wanted to step a bit further from what I was used to.

My second experiment was with Pop. I decided I wanted to give it a fairer shake and actually run it from a partition on my machine rather than starving it on a flash drive as I had with Mint. I set up a small partition for Pop alongside my Windows installation partition and began the install. Pop comes with GNOME or (soon) COSMIC. It is an amicable install complete with GUI, hand-holding, and minimal questions. At this point I ran into two issues:

  1. After playing with GNOME, I realized I was more interested in trying KDE
  2. I could no longer access my Windows install

The first was a useful realization, but the second was and is a bit of an issue. I discovered at that point that Pop is in theory fairly easy to dual boot with Windows if you are using EFI partitions. I did not do that. I was using a legacy BIOS which I have not yet been willing to upgrade to UEFI out of fear of an incredibly unlikely but not unprecedented temporary and localized power outage. Universe, I would like to request a UPS for my birthday.

Pivoting to Arch

While building up courage to convert my BIOS to UEFI, I decided to go in a completely new direction and install Arch Linux on another drive. This is a complete pivot in that it is not even slightly beginner friendly, and it has also gone surprisingly well.

To be continued

item.title: Chorizo Soup
item.description: Spicy chorizo makes a refreshing soup that's good year-round.
item.content:encoded:
Servings & Time

Makes 10ish bowls / fills the red pot. Assume around 3 hours in the kitchen, as you need to chop veggies, cook meat, and clean up.

Choosing Ingredients

Chorizo is the star of this soup. It’s packed full of flavor, so you don’t have to work as hard to come up with flavors on your own. Look for fresh sausages from the butcher if possible.

Chicken thighs are used to bolster the soup and add protein while not going quite as hard on cholesterol as a chorizo-only soup would. Thigh meat stands up to cooking down in soup better than breast does, so we prefer it to breast meat here. Bone-in thighs also have more flavor, so I use those and do the extra work of deboning and shredding at the end of the recipe. If you want to skip deboning, you can just use boneless thighs instead.

Marinade

  • 2-4 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp black pepper
  • 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1 tsp oregano
  • 1 tsp garlic powder

Ingredients

  • 1lb chorizo sausage, casings removed
  • 4 chicken thighs, trimmed & whole
  • 1 lb carrots, chopped
  • 1 lb radishes, matchsticked
  • 1 large onion, chopped
  • 6+ cloves garlic, minced
  • 1-2 lbs baby red potatoes, halved
  • 1 can corn, drained
  • 1 can navy beans, drained
  • 64 oz chicken broth
  • 8 oz cream cheese
  • 1 bunch cilantro, chopped
  • 1 lb orzo pasta
  • 3-4 limes

Seasonings to Taste

  • salt
  • chili powder
  • smoked paprika
  • garlic
  • onion powder
  • oregano
  • cumin

Marination Directions

Marinate your chicken thighs in a thin coating of extra virgin olive oil. Season with salt, black pepper, garlic powder, oregano, and a healthy coating of paprika & massage it in. Let it chill in the fridge while you chop your veggies.

Soup Directions

  1. Brown your chicken in a skillet on medium heat (6) with a thin coating of olive oil. Don’t worry about cooking it all the way through - this is just to add flavor. Set it aside.
  2. In your stew pot, heat the olive oil on medium heat (6). Add the onion and cook till softened. Add the garlic and cook until the onion starts to brown.
  3. Add the chorizo to the pot and break it up. Once the chorizo starts to brown, add in the chicken broth, chicken, potatoes, beans, corn, and carrots. Wait on the radishes - they go in at the end. Bring it up to a boil and then reduce to a med-low simmer.
  4. While your soup is simmering, fill a sauce pot up about half way with water and bring it up to a boil and add in the orzo. Cook until al dente.
  5. After it’s been simmering at least 10-15 minutes, the sausage should be safe - start tasting your soup. Depending on the sausage used, you may want to modify the flavor. Consider adding more salt, smoked paprika, garlic, onion powder, oregano, or cumin. For a mild spice kick add more chili powder, or for a moderate kick add in cayenne or chipotle powder. Try a half a teaspoon of these at a time.
  6. Once the chicken is shreddable and the potatoes are done, cut off the heat, shred the chicken, and then stir in the cream cheese & radishes - I like the crisp taste radishes have if you don’t cook them much. Allow it to cool for a few minutes.
  7. Serve over the orzo & garnish with cilantro & lime wedges.

Try

Try marinating the chicken longer.

It might be nice to add in peppers with the onions, this soup seems like it would get along well with peppers. Also maybe more beans.

If you like sour, zesting the limes before cutting them and adding the zest either to the soup directly or as a garnish would probably work.

item.title: Fall Braised Pork
item.description: My recipe for braised pork is sweet and autumnal.
item.content:encoded:
Servings & Time

Makes 10-15 servings. Start a day and a half before you want to eat it as it will sit in the refrigerator, then the oven, for a very long time.

This goes well on rice or sandwiches, with fresh slaw or a salad.

Brine Ingredients - use a beer bottle to avoid dishes :)

  • 48oz Yuengling beer (4 beer bottles)
  • 32oz apple cider (3-4 beer bottles)
  • 80-92oz water (7-8 beer bottles)
  • 12oz sugar (1 beer bottle)
  • 12oz salt (1 beer bottle)
  • 1 tbsp cloves

Braised Pork Ingredients

  • 1 8-10lb brined pork shoulder
  • 24 oz chopped carrots
  • 6-8 celery sticks, chopped
  • 2 large onions, chopped
  • 1 peach, sliced (optional)
  • 24-32 oz Yuengling beer (2-3 beer bottles)
  • 24-32 oz apple cider
  • 1 drizzle of Worcestershire sauce (at least a few tablespoons)
  • 2+ tbsp salt
  • 2+ tbsp pepper
  • 1+ tbsp brown sugar
  • 1 dusting of paprika
  • 1 dusting of allspice
  • 3+ tbsp pork rub of your choice
  • 2-3 tbsp of a high-heat tolerant oil

Peach Sauce Ingredients

  • 3 peaches, skinned and chopped
  • 1-3 shots of bourbon whiskey
  • 2-3 tablespoons brown sugar

Brining Directions

  1. Prepare your pork shoulder. If yours was frozen, it only needs to be partially thawed before brining, as the thaw time can incorporate into the brine time.
  2. Rub the shoulder down with the dry ingredients first, poking the cloves into the meat.
  3. Set the shoulder into a large stock pot, then slowly pour the wet ingredients into the pot around the shoulder to avoid disturbing the rub, alternating alcohol & cider with water to keep the 50/50 water/not water ratio consistent.
  4. Leave it in the refrigerator for 8-24 hours.

Braising Directions

  1. Cut your oven up to 275 degrees F.
  2. Move your chopped vegetables into the braising pan and make a nice bed for the meat.
  3. Retrieve your brined shoulder and drain the brine. Rub it down with a healthy coating of salt, pepper, and a nice pork rub. I had one on hand that was a garlicky mesquite, with smoked paprika, brown sugar, etc.
  4. Get your largest skillet roaring hot, then pour in a drizzle of oil that handles heat well and drop the meat on there.
  5. Laugh because your skillet is too small and you don’t have the correct tools to flip the meat. That’s ok, just carefully move the meat with your hands. The shoulder is large enough that by the time you get each side seared, a different side is cool enough to grab without burning yourself.
    • Alternately, you could have the correct tool, probably a salad claw or some grilling tongs.
    • Alternately, you can skip this step. Searing does add to the flavor, but this recipe is still highly edible without it.
    • I wash my hands a lot while cooking and you probably should too.
  6. Relocate your now seared and fragrant pork to its veggie bed in the braising pan, fat cap side up. The fat will baste the rest of the meat while cooking and help to keep it moist.
  7. Pour beer and apple cider into the braising pan until it’s been filled 1/3 to 1/2 of the way up. Keep in mind that the pork will release a lot of liquid, and if you fill the dish too high it may overflow. If you like, arrange some peach slices on top of the pork. They will cook down to nothing, but the juice should incorporate nicely.
  8. Cover the dish and pop it in the oven for 5-6 hours, checking every so often to make sure that the liquid levels are good and to check the doneness.
  9. Once it seems to be around 2/3 of the way done, slice a crisscross pattern into the top and pat in a few tablespoons of brown sugar, a dusting of paprika and allspice, and a nice drizzle of Worcestershire sauce. Put it back in for another hour or so, or until you can easily tear off pieces with a fork. You’ll want it somewhere between roast and pulled pork consistency.
  10. Let it rest, begin prepping sauce.
  11. Serve with rice and a dollop of peach sauce.

Peach Sauce Directions

  1. Heat a small sauce pot on medium-low (4) heat.
  2. Add the peaches to the pot with a splash or 3 of bourbon, then slowly incorporate the brown sugar to taste.
  3. Cook down until the sauce reaches a pleasant spreading consistency and the alcohol taste of the bourbon is gone.

Try

Try pureeing the peaches before adding them into the sauce pot. This brings them to a sauce-like consistency faster, and allows you to make a thinner sauce if desired because you won’t have to cook out as much liquid to get it spreadable.

Try adding cracked black pepper, chili pepper, or cayenne pepper to the sauce. Spiced fruit is always a winner.

item.title: Loaded Baked Potato Soup
item.description: I can survive off of this baked potato soup for a week straight with no complaints.
item.content:encoded:
Servings & Time

Makes 8 respectable bowls, it’s about 3 hours in the kitchen if you count bacon, veggie chopping, and cleanup.

Choosing Ingredients

Pick your potato of choice. Oftentimes, I go with red potatoes because I like their texture. However, a grainier, starchier potato will soften up and break down into the soup a little more, so if you like a thick, starchy soup, a russet potato may be to your preference.

I like to add summer sausage to this soup. It adds so much flavor when seared. You can leave it out - 1 lb of bacon is plenty of meat already - or sub it for a different sausage with a flavor you prefer. I can imagine any non-sweet breakfast sausage, italian sausage, or chorizo would be delightful.

Ingredients

  • 2-3 lbs potatoes, cut into 1.5 inch pieces
  • 1 lb bacon
  • 8oz summer sausage
  • 1 yellow onion, chopped
  • 5 sticks celery, chopped
  • 1 c carrots, chopped
  • 1 head broccoli, break up florets into spoon-friendly pieces
  • 1 heaping tbsp grated garlic
  • 48 oz chicken broth
  • 5 heaping tbs. flour
  • 4 tbsp butter
  • 2 cups of milk
  • 1 cup of shredded cheddar
  • garlic powder to taste
  • salt to taste
  • black pepper to taste

Toppings

  • smoked paprika to taste
  • 1 bundle of green onions, chopped
  • 16 oz sour cream

Directions

  1. Cook the bacon to a decent crisp and set it aside to cool. Save or toss most of the grease but leave a coating in the pan. If you don’t like bacon grease, olive oil works with the flavors of this soup. Sear the sausage in the same pan and set it aside as well. If you used summer sausage it’s already cooked, so you just want to add some browning to bring out the flavor.
  2. Add the onion to the bacon pan on medium (6) and cook until the onion is translucent.
  3. Move the onion to the soup pot. Add the chicken broth and potatoes and get it bubbling gently on medium-high heat (7-8) for 10 mins.
  4. Add all chopped veggies except the onion greens & broccoli. Cut down the heat to medium (6).
  5. After another 5-10 mins add salt, pepper, and garlic powder to taste. Add the broccoli and reduce heat to medium-low (4). The earlier you add in the broccoli, the more it will break down into your soup.
  6. In the meantime, lazy rinse the bacon pan (the onions should have more or less deglazed it already) and chop the bacon.
  7. Make a light roux in the bacon pan - add the butter and milk and slowly whisk (or sift) in flour. Do your best to keep it smooth. If it comes out lumpy, that’s OK! You can either accept the lumps, which will be disguised by the potatoes, or you can blend them together with an immersion blender. Add cheddar cheese in after the milk is combined. You want it to thicken up mildly - think pudding, but not hummus.
  8. The veggies should be cooked and the potatoes should be fork-tender. The broth should have boiled down a fair bit such that some of the veggies poke above the surface. Stir in the roux, bacon, and garlic and cook for a few minutes until it is thoroughly combined. Keeping in mind that it will continue to thicken after it is taken off the heat, remove it from heat before it reaches the desired consistency. Let it cool, stirring every few mins, until it reaches an edible temperature.
  9. Top with onion greens, smoked paprika, and sour cream and serve.

Alternative - Loaded Chicken & Potato Soup

Near the end, add in cooked chicken as well. You can either cook it and season it yourself or use a rotisserie bird. Like with sausage, any seasoning from your meat will contribute to the soup, so keep spices harmonious. If you aren’t adventurous, a standard standard holiday bird combo of salt, pepper, rosemary, thyme, and sage will work. Cook it until it’s just barely done in the bacon grease or olive oil. If your chicken is refrigerated, add it in a few minutes before you remove the soup from heat. If it’s hot off the stove, add it in after it’s been removed from the heat and allow residual heat from the soup to finish it.

You can also add frozen peas around the time you’d add broccoli.

You could also try using ranch seasoning instead of the base seasonings. It feels correct.
